newsitem.title: USA: Steady Fed may pave way for further dollar slide.
newsitem.headline: Steady Fed may pave way for further dollar slide.

text.p: A Federal Reserve decision to hold interest rates steady could pave the way for an already battle-weary dollar to tumble even further, analysts said.
The greenback sank to a five-month low of 111.98 yen in overseas trading on Tuesday as dollar bears weighed the risk of a near-term hike in official Japanese rates.
News that the Fed decided to sit on its hands contrasted with that growing speculation of higher Japanese rates.
"So, this has to mean that the currency will move in favor of the Japanese yen. And the dollar, I think, will slide," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp.
"I wouldn't be surprised at all if the yen approaches 110 (per dollar) fairly soon," Sohn added.

The Bank of Japan (BOJ) has left its official discount rate (ODR) at a record low 0.5 percent since September 1995 to help bolster growth. By contrast, the U.S. federal funds rate is at 5.50 percent and the discount rate at 5.0 percent.

The differential between rates in Japan and the United States helped power the dollar to a 56-month high of 127.46 yen on May 1. But since then, the ailing U.S. currency has lost some 12 percent versus the Japanese unit.
Sohn said it is about time for the BOJ to hike. "Their rates are too low, and if they keep up the current levels, they will have more inflation on their hands later," he added.
Burtle said there was very little chance for a cut in interest rates in Germany, while German rates may rise towards the end of the year.
The German discount rate stands at 2.50 percent.
Burtle's year-end forecast calls for the dollar to fetch around 1.60 marks.
After the Fed announcement on Tuesday, the dollar fell as low as 1.6755 marks and 112.50 yen compared to 1.6995/05 marks and 113.80/90 yen shortly before the central bank statement.
Some experts wondered if the dollar could come under further pressure when trading gets underway in Japan overnight.
Elliott Dix, assistant vice president at Signet Bank, said the Fed's inaction indicated the central bank has more time to see evidence of a slowdown.
"We may have only seen a one-time hike here," he said. "And, I think, the market might be pricing in that potential."
Dix said there was a chance for weakness in the dollar overnight if a comparable amount of participants in the Japanese market shared that fear.
Fed policymakers had raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25, the first increase in more than two years.
